profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at a mid-size cloud infrastructure company that operates a distributed object storage service. Over the past week, several enterprise customers have reported intermittent spikes in read latency after the team enabled a Stardust-style end-to-end tracing pipeline in production for a subset of traffic. The meeting is between the storage platform engineer responsible for the tracing rollout and the site reliability engineer responsible for production health. Their agenda is to diagnose whether the latency spike is caused by the tracing system itself, by a storage-path regression merely revealed by tracing, or by how the collected traces are being processed, and to decide on an immediate mitigation and a short follow-up investigation. The expected outcome is an agreed troubleshooting plan for 'rolling back the problematic part' and 'verifying the fix' before the next peak-traffic window.

members.name: Lena Park
members.expertise: Distributed storage internals, request-path instrumentation, latency analysis
members.background: Lena designed much of the recent Stardust-inspired tracing integration for the object storage service and previously worked on RPC middleware and storage-node scheduling.
members.private_state: She wants to avoid a full rollback of tracing because leadership sees the rollout as strategically important, and she suspects the issue is in downstream trace export or interpretation rather than the in-band instrumentation hooks.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'tracing is on,' they mean the lightweight in-process span emission path is enabled, not necessarily that every span is exported immediately to the analytics pipeline.
The 'read latency spike' under discussion refers to the service's internal p99 from request admission to final byte scheduled, because that is the dashboard she uses for storage-path regressions.
If they agree to 'turn tracing back,' the intended scope is disabling the new remote export and query fan-out components while preserving local span capture for diagnosis.
A 'verified fix' means the p99 returns to the pre-rollout weekday baseline during a representative canary window, even if a small number of long-tail outliers remain.
The 'current rollout' refers to the canary cohort on the east-region metadata and object nodes that received the new async exporter package on Tuesday night.

members.name: Marco Silva
members.expertise: Production monitoring, incident response, capacity analysis, SLO enforcement
members.background: Marco runs reliability reviews for the storage platform and owns the dashboards, alerts, and mitigation playbooks used during customer-facing performance incidents.
members.private_state: He wants a fast, low-risk mitigation before the next customer traffic surge and is concerned that any instrumentation overhead affecting tail latency will trigger another SLO breach, even if the root cause is analytically interesting.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'tracing is on,' they mean end-to-end tracing is fully active from request tagging through collector ingest and backend writes, because that's the only state that matters operationally.
The 'read latency spike' means customer-observed p99.9 time from client first byte sent to full response completion on the external SLO dashboard.
If they agree to 'turn tracing back,' the obvious action is to remove tracing headers and span generation from request handling on the canary traffic entirely.
A 'verified fix' means customer-facing alerts stay green through one full peak period and the p99.9 stays under the formal SLO threshold, not just near historical baseline.
The 'current rollout' refers to all traffic in the east region routed through the ingress fleet after the sampler was changed globally via config on Wednesday morning.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss whether 'tracing being on' is causing the latency issue.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Lena means the request path is generating spans locally with lightweight hooks; export and backend processing are separable and may be the real source of overhead.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marco means the full tracing stack is active, including propagation, collector ingest, and storage writes; if any of that is active, tracing is 'on.'
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In many engineering conversations 'tracing on/off' is treated as a single operational state, so each assumes the other is using the common shorthand rather than a narrower subsystem definition.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They repeatedly refer to 'the spike we saw yesterday' and 'the read latency graph.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Lena is thinking of an internal storage-service p99 panel covering admission-to-dispatch latency on the east canary cluster.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marco is thinking of the customer-facing p99.9 SLO panel showing end-to-end client latency across east-region ingress traffic.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both dashboards are well known and both showed anomalies around the same time, so references to 'the spike' feel unambiguous even though each person mentally anchors on a different graph and percentile.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree they may need to 'turn tracing back' before peak traffic.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Lena assumes this means disabling the async exporter, collector fan-out, and heavy query-side enrichment while leaving local spans and trace IDs in place for continued diagnosis.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marco assumes this means removing tracing from live request handling altogether for the affected traffic, including header propagation and span creation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Rollback language in incidents is often intentionally compressed for speed, and both options are plausibly described as 'turning tracing back,' so the hidden difference in boundaries never gets surfaced.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to 'verify the fix'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They align on the need to 'verify the fix' after mitigation.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Lena believes verification is a short canary comparison showing p99 returns near pre-rollout baseline and trace pipeline backpressure disappears.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marco believes verification requires surviving a full demand peak with no customer-facing SLO alert recurrence at p99.9.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Verification is a standard phrase that usually sounds self-explanatory; because both expect some follow-up observation after the change, they do not notice they are applying different sufficiency thresholds and time horizons.

turns.inner_thought: The east canary that got the new async exporter package Tuesday night is the only rollout slice I really trust for signal here. On my storage dashboard, the internal p99 from admission to final byte scheduled definitely jumped after rollout, but the request-path hooks themselves still look lightweight. I need to frame this as an isolation problem, not a reason to rip out the whole tracing effort.
turns.utterance: Thanks for jumping on. Since the Stardust rollout, we did see a read latency spike on the east canary, and I want to separate whether tracing being on is actually causing it or whether we're just seeing another issue more clearly now.

turns.inner_thought: What matters to me is the customer-facing p99.9 on the east-region ingress fleet after the Wednesday sampler change. That spike lined up with the SLO alerts yesterday afternoon. If tracing is on end to end and customers feel it, I don't really care yet which component is philosophically at fault.
turns.utterance: Yeah, my main concern is the spike customers would actually feel. Tracing being on lines up pretty closely with the alert window from yesterday afternoon, at least from what the read latency graph showed.

turns.inner_thought: The in-process span emission path barely moved CPU in the canary samples. The pressure smells more like export backlog or downstream handling than storage-path regression from instrumentation itself. If I can keep people from equating all of tracing with the request-path hooks, we might avoid a blunt rollback.
turns.utterance: From the data I've checked so far, the request-path hooks looked cheap in canary. My current read is that tracing being on may be surfacing pressure around the collector or export side rather than adding much in the core path.

turns.inner_thought: If the end-to-end tracing stack is active anywhere along the live request path, that's enough risk for me. I need the lowest-risk mitigation before evening traffic. We can debate collector versus propagation later; for incident purposes it all counts as tracing being on, and turning tracing back should mean getting it out of live canary traffic entirely.
turns.utterance: Maybe, but if tracing is on and it's contributing anywhere in the chain, I don't especially care which segment owns the overhead right now. Before peak traffic, I just want the customer-visible latency removed.

turns.inner_thought: Best immediate move is to turn tracing back by disabling exporter fan-out and the heavier downstream path while leaving local span capture intact. That keeps diagnostic value and should relieve the pipeline backpressure if I'm right. Then I can compare the internal p99 read latency graph against Tuesday baseline during the canary window.
turns.utterance: In that case, I think we should turn tracing back for now, then compare the read latency graph after the change and see if the spike settles.

turns.inner_thought: Good, we're aligned: turn tracing back on the affected east traffic before the evening surge, meaning remove it from request handling so we stop paying any tail-latency tax. I need this done fast and clean, not as a partial experiment that leaves the risky bits in place.
turns.utterance: Agreed. Turning tracing back makes sense, and I'd like the affected east traffic cleaned up before the evening surge starts.

turns.inner_thought: After the rollback on the canary nodes, I want to verify the fix by seeing p99 return near the pre-rollout weekday baseline and confirming the trace pipeline queues stop backing up. That's sufficient to show the exporter path was the problem, even if a few outliers remain.
turns.utterance: Once that's applied, we should verify the fix by checking whether the read latency graph is back near Tuesday baseline and whether the queueing we've been watching drops.

turns.inner_thought: I need more than a quick rebound on an internal panel. To verify the fix for incident purposes, the customer alert board has to stay green through at least the next peak hour and the external p99.9 needs to stay under the SLO line. Otherwise we're just congratulating ourselves too early.
turns.utterance: Yes, and I want to verify the fix against the customer alert board through the next peak hour too, so we know the issue is actually gone and not just quieter for a few minutes.

turns.inner_thought: If turning tracing back doesn't move the internal read-path p99 on the east canary, then the tracing hooks probably only exposed an existing bottleneck, likely around the metadata-node read path or scheduling interactions. I should plant that next step now so we don't default to blaming instrumentation forever.
turns.utterance: And if the spike is still there after tracing is back, then I'd want us to look hard at the metadata-node read path, because tracing may have just exposed an existing bottleneck.

turns.inner_thought: I'll write this up as immediate rollback of tracing on east traffic, then hold the incident open until we've made it through peak without another customer-facing breach. If that stays clean, we can call it stable; if not, we escalate into the storage path. What matters is a mitigation now and a clear verification gate.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll update the incident notes that we're turning tracing back immediately and will verify the fix before we declare things stable.
